headline: “This year” is spelled with 今, “now” — but the word began with 此, “this”.
A tip and a chip share one katakana spelling but two different English words.
A pun or witticism is the stem of a verb for “stylish” — spelled with kanji that were fitted to the sound.
Kana orthography is “kana use” — and the つかい voices to づかい.
Coal is “rock charcoal” — a native word that was later re-read in Chinese sounds.
To permit is to make something “loose”.
To notice is for awareness to “stick” — つく voiced to づく.
“To move” may start from the sound of something wriggling.
“Skilful” is, in Chinese, “top hand” — and this reading mixes two layers of Chinese sounds.
Chalk has a Japanese twin in チャコ.
Pale is “blue-white” — and the しろい voices to じろい on the way in.
Twenty years old is an Old Japanese “twenty items” — read as a single old word, not as nijū + sai.
“Time” is the moon (or month) and the sun (or day), side by side.
“Abundance” arrived from written Chinese, and is first attested in Japanese in the 1830s.
“Again” is “two” plus a counter for “times”.
To protect is to “watch over”, and its first syllable is an old word for “eye”.
A glove is a “hand bag”, with ふくろ voiced to ぶくろ.
“A.M.” is “before noon”.
A lens may have come through Dutch or English — Wiktionary says it can't be sure which.
To be revived is, literally, to “return from the land of the dead”.
An actor's lines may be a “calling out” — and the kanji came from a different, Chinese-derived word.
“Possible” is “may” plus “able” — borrowed whole from Middle Chinese.
A memory is a “thought” that has “come out”.
Lunch, or noon, is a beautified “daytime”.
A serious face may be one with nervous, blinking eyes — and the kanji only fake the logic.
A crowd got its おお from native Japanese, grafted onto a Chinese word.
ナンバー has a twin in Japanese: ノンブル.
“Nostalgic” first meant wanting to keep something close — and only later became about remembering.
To change clothes is to “put on” and “exchange” — with the かえる voicing to がえる.
“Effort” is, in Chinese, “to exert strength”.
“Docile” is “adult” plus an adjective-forming ending.
